Title: Understory Environmental Conditions Drive Leaf Level‐Lipid Biosynthesis in a Deciduous and Evergreen Tree Species
URL Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11788954/
Markdown Content:
Plants in the understory experience climatic conditions affected by the overstory canopy that influence physiological and biochemical processes.

Here, we investigate the relationships of leaf lipid molecular abundances to leaf water content, transmitted irradiance, and free‐air temperature (_T_ air) from deciduous angiosperm (_Quercus buckleyi_) and evergreen gymnosperm (_Juniperus ashei_) understory trees across an elevation gradient in a central Texas (USA) woodland.
Monthly sampling from 04/2019 to 01/2020 revealed that long‐chain leaf waxes (≥ C 27) accumulated with leaf water deficit over the growing season for both tree species.
Higher transmitted light during the hottest, driest months was due to a decreased leaf area index (LAI) in the canopy as leaf shedding is a common drought response.
Isoprenoids (sesqui‐, di‐terpenoids, phytosterols) in leaves changed by month with changing LAI and transmittance associated with monthly _T_ air changes.
The chain length of _n_‐alkanols in _Q. buckleyi_ shifted with seasonal LAI at different topographic positions.
The unsaturation of fatty acids in both tree species decreased with increased seasonal _T_ air but showed topography sensitivity.
Leaf‐level metabolites responded to understory microclimatic variables that were influenced by seasonality and topography.
**Keywords:** deciduous species, evergreen species, leaf lipid biosynthesis, leaf terpenoids, leaf wax, understory environments
Summary statement
The woodland understory environment constrains the leaf lipid biochemistry of trees during the growing season, differing by plant water‐use strategy.
Seasonal dynamics in leaf waxes, terpenoids, and phytosterols produced in _Juniperus ashei_ and _Quercus buckleyi_ leaves responded most strongly to summer drought and varied by topographic position.

Temperature, light and water availability influence leaf photosynthetic processes (e.g., Berry and Bjorkman 1980; Poorter et al.2019; Wang et al.2022), change biochemical reaction rates, regulate the secondary metabolic process (Qaderi, Martel, and Strugnell 2023), and impact primary productivity and carbon cycles in the ecosystem (e.g., Anderson‐Teixeira et al.2011; Poorter et al.2019).
Plant lipids have essential ecological roles as major constituents for cuticles, lipid membrane structure and energy providers for the various metabolic processes (e.g., Kim 2020).

It is well known that plants adjust their lipid molecular composition and distribution in response to variations in temperature (Narayanan et al.2016; Shiva et al.2020), light (Shepherd and Griffiths 2006), and plant water (Xue et al.2017).

For example, leaf cuticular wax, as the protective layer between the atmosphere and leaves, is increased with exposure to ultraviolet radiation, as chain lengths of the homologs are shifted to shorter chain lengths at higher irradiance (Tevini and Steinmüller 1987).
The content of leaf wax is also affected by drought stress with increased expression of wax biosynthesis genes (Kosma et al.2009).

Within the mesophyll tissue, fatty acid unsaturation is decreased such as lower amounts of α‐linolenic acid and oleic acid with coincident increased amounts of saturated fatty acids (SFAs) (e.g., palmitic acid) in response to high‐temperature stress via regulation of fatty acid desaturases enzyme activity (Zoong Lwe et al.2021).

In rice seedlings, β‐sitosterol concentration is increased proportionally to the severity of drought stress due to an upregulated expression of the sterol biosynthesis and metabolisms (e.g., hydroxy‐3‐methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase) (Kumar et al.2015).
Diterpenoids accumulate in foliage with increasing drought and oxidative stress as a transcriptional expression of the diterpenoid synthases is induced (Mafu et al.2018).
However, little is known about the seasonality of leaf lipid metabolism especially within the understory of forests and woodlands (Wang, White, and Hockaday 2024).
The microclimate of the understory is moderated by the overstory canopy, affecting biological and ecological processes (De Frenne et al.2019; Haesen et al.2021).

Generally overstory canopy constrains environmental conditions in the understory primarily through leaf area development affecting above canopy diurnal and seasonal changes in evapotranspiration cooling associated with soil water availability, and absorbed insolation (e.g., Lenoir et al.2013; De Frenne et al.2019).
In addition, localized topographic gradients (e.g., slope and elevation) further influence canopy development and stratification.
Typically, understory trees may experience lower ground‐level temperatures, higher relative humidity, and lower shortwave incoming radiation (e.g., von Arx et al.2013).

For example, Zellweger et al. (2019) found summer maximum temperatures in a temperate deciduous canopy were 2.1°C cooler than that of the outside of the canopy which was strongly related to the local canopy structure.
The magnitude of the canopy cooling effect may vary seasonally (Aalto et al.2022), likely buffering the understory environment for the vegetation during climate extremes (e.g., De Frenne et al.2019).
The seasonality effects may exert natural selective and interactive stresses on trees and subsequently on their physiological responses.

Seasonal variations in temperature, precipitation, humidity and day length constrain the microenvironment of both overstory and understory trees (Lisovski, Ramenofsky, and Wingfield 2017) which is affected by topographic position (Feakins et al.2016).
The seasonality represented by general topographic patterns may not reflect the exact seasonality that the individual plants have experienced in their microhabitat.

Lastly, tree species have unique individual water use strategies affecting their tissue moisture content and transpiration rates related to mechanisms regulating leaf stomatal responses to high temperature and drought stress (Li et al.2016; Richter et al.2022).

Unsurprisingly, given the combination of factors including the understory microclimate, the position of forest stands within complex terrain, and differences in water use by individual tree species, little is known about the types of leaf lipids that responded (e.g., Speckert, Petibon, and Wiesenberg 2023).

Here, we characterized the molecular composition and abundance of leaf lipids of two cooccurring tree species expressing different water‐use strategies growing in the understory of a forest at three topographic positions in response to transmitted light, leaf water content, and temperature, over a growing season.

Drawing on previous work, Wang, White, and Hockaday (2024) found leaf wax average chain length decreased, less unsaturated fatty acids (UFAs), and unique isoprenoid production were associated with higher temperatures in a forest understory.

Because temperature covaries seasonally with irradiance and water availability related to the topographic position, we endeavor to test whether similar patterns in leaf lipid biosynthesis are also affected by these environmental factors.

Specifically, we test whether: (1) leaf lipid profiles of the tree species varied differently both monthly and seasonally in response to irradiance and leaf water content changing understory microclimate (Figure 1); and (2) the topographic positions of the two tree species have different lipid composition highlighting the influence of the local environment on biochemical processes (Figure 1).

This study is important for interpreting lipid compounds found in geologic sediments for reconstructing the paleoclimate of past forests and providing insights into the lipid synthesis responses associated with environmental factors related to the current climatic change.

Materials and Methods
Site Descriptions

This study quantified the leaf lipids from deciduous angiosperm (_Quercus. buckleyi_) and evergreen gymnosperm (_Juniperus ashei_) trees growing in the understory of a subtropical woodland in central Texas (William Cameron Park, Waco, Texas, 31°35′1.32″ N latitude, 97°9′22.68″ W longitude).
The selected species of _Q. buckleyi_ and _J. ashei_ have different water reservation strategies.

The woodlands of this park are distributed over hilly terrain dominated by the oak–juniper species with shallow, rocky soils in the uplands to deeper soils in the lowlands, that are rich in clay minerals (Archer and Bratton 2010).
The climate is classified as humid subtropical with a mean annual temperature of 19.5°C (1970–2020) and mean annual precipitation of 87.9 cm (1970–2020) (https://www.weather.gov/fwd/actclimo).

Fresh leaves of _Q. buckleyi_ and _J. ashei_ were collected for approximately one growing season from five different locations along a slope gradient of 5° within Cameron Park (Supporting Information S1: Figure S1).
These sampling sites were selected representing different topographic positions (i.e., upland, midslope, and lowland) (Supporting Information S1: Figure S1).
These sites represent a gradient of associated site water availability and are primarily associated with soil development across the hilly terrain (Supporting Information S1: Figure S2).
Soils of the upland and midslope sites are shallow (< 25 cm overlying limestone bedrock), gravelly clay loams of the Eddy‐Stephen soil complex.

The lowland site is situated on Weswood series soil, a deep loamy fluvial entisol on the Bosque River floodplain approximately 1 m above the water table (Soil Survey of McLennan County, Texas, 2001) (https://maps.lib.utexas.edu/maps/soil_surveys/mclennan_county_text_2001.pdf).
Plant‐available water storage within the upper 25 cm is estimated to be 1.5 cm in the upland soils, 2.0 cm in midslope soils, and 8.0 cm in the lowlands (Soil Survey Staff 2019).
The range of soil depths and soil water storage establishes a gradient of soil moisture and associated edaphic factors as a function of topography position.
The trees in the upland and midslope were grown in the middle of small opening woods while those in the lowland were grown along the open trial next to the local tributary.
At each site, leaves showing no visible sign of insect or physical damage were sampled from one _Q. buckleyi_ tree (mean tree height 2–2.5 m) and one _J. ashei_ tree (mean tree height 3–5 m).
The leaves were collected from the same sampling point and the same tree across the growing season to make the lipid profile results consistent and comparable.
Branches from both species projected nearly perpendicular from the tree stem with leaves inserting generally laterally from the branch.

Approximately 1 g of two foliage samples was sampled monthly at the inside of branches along a horizontal axis and at the edge (~1.5 m above the forest floor) of the selected trees to obtain a nearly representative sample of leaves exposed to varying light conditions.
Leaf samples of the deciduous _Q. buckleyi_ were collected monthly from April 2019 to October 2019 (_n_ = 5 × 2 × 7 = 70).
For the evergreen _J. ashei_, leaves were collected monthly from April 2019 to October 2019 and January 2020 (_n_ = 5 × 2 × 8 = 80).
Measurement of Environmental Factors
Understory Light Measurement
The leaf‐level transmitted irradiance (μmol m−2 s−1) was quantified using the LAI‐2000 plant canopy analyzer (_LI‐COR_ Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA).
We isolated maximum direct beam irradiance by using the radiation measured at angles of 0° to 15° in post‐processing of the LAI‐2000 data.
Diffuse radiation from the other zenith angles (16° to 74°) was excluded as it was considered a minor portion of the total irradiance received by the leaves and an undesired source of variance.
Leaf area index (LAI; m 2 leaf m−2 ground) is a measurement of the quantity of the foliage area in a plant canopy per unit ground area.
For our study, we measured the LAI of the canopy using the LAI‐2000 and utilizing all measurement angles.

This was accomplished by taking 5 sampling points above each tree of which leaves were collected for phytochemical analysis in the early morning (~9 to 11 am) at clear sky conditions, once per month from April 2019 to January 2020.
Both transmitted irradiance and LAI were recorded monthly at each sampling site, denoting light transmittance and LAI sites, respectively.
Here, the monthly LAI values were the mean values calculated from each sampling site as a measurement of seasonal variation in the whole forest canopy structure.

Ambient Monthly Meteorology

Monthly free‐air maximum (_T_ max) and minimum temperature (_T_ min) and precipitation data were obtained from the Waco Reginal Airport (Texas, USA, USW00013959, elevation: 152 m, 31°37′8.04″ N latitude, 97°13′41.88″ W longitude) accessed from the National Centers for Environmental Information archived by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
The monthly temperature and precipitation data used in our analysis was an average of daily values.

To understand the temperature difference within the canopy, outside of the canopy, and free‐air temperature measured at the local meteorological weather station (Texas, USA, USW00013959, elevation: 152 m, 31°37′8.04″ N latitude, 97°13′41.88″ W longitude), we measured the temperatures in the canopy (_n_ = 4) and outside of the canopy (_n_ = 4) at each sampling site at 1.0 m above the forest floor using a thermometer (OAKTON Temp300, Eutech, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA) at two selected time points, 4 April 2021 (9:40 to 10:50 am) and 8 September 2021 (10:00 to 11:20 am) (Supporting Information S1: Figure S4).

The collected leaves were put into plastic bags and placed into a thermos cooler with ice during transportation to the laboratory.
The leaf fresh weight (mg) was measured ≤ 6 h after the leaf was clipped from each sampling point.
The turgid weight (mg) was determined on a subset of leaves in each sample by immersion in deionized water (DIW) at room temperature until they reached a constant weight, typically 18 h.

Specifically, the _Q. buckleyi_ leaves were emersed with their petioles facing downwards in the DIW while the _J. ashei_ needles were emersed in DIW as each needle at a sampling point was placed into a separate Petri dish.
Leaf surfaces were gently patted dry with a lint‐free towel before weighing.
Dry weight (mg) was determined after placing the leaf into aluminum trays for oven‐dry at 90°C for 10 h.
Leaves used for this process were excluded from the lipid analyses described in Section 2.3.
Leaf Sample Preparation and Lipid Extraction and Fractionation
Collected leaf samples were subsequently freeze‐dried and then powdered with an herb mill.

To prevent sample transfer‐ and cross‐contamination, the mill was extensively cleaned between samples 5 to 10 times rinsing the chamber and blades with a mixture of acetone and methanol (v/v, 1:1), wiping with a lint‐free disposable towel, followed by flushing with compressed nitrogen gas.
The powdered samples were stored in a freezer (−18 to −25°C) until further analysis.

Homogenized fresh leaf samples (~100 mg) were extracted and fractionated using accelerated solvent extraction (ASE; Dionex 200) inserted with a layer of activated silica gel (oven‐activated at 200°C for 4 h immediately before use) (60 Å HYD 40‐63 µm, VWR, PA, USA) over three extraction cycles at 1500 psi and 100°C as details described in Wang et al. (2022).

The methodological details, measured efficiency, and recovery rates were presented in Wang et al. (2022).Obtaining the maximum lipid extraction yields from each tree species required the use of slightly differing solvent mixtures (Wang, White, and Hockaday 2024).

For _Q. buckleyi_, the free lipids were successively extracted and fractionated using an ASE with _n_‐hexane: dichloromethane (DCM) (80:20, v/v) to get hydrocarbons, esters, and alcohols followed with _n_‐hexane: DCM: methanol (MeOH) (40:50:10, v/v/v) to get alcohols and acids.

For _J. ashei_, the free lipids were sequentially extracted and fractionated with _n_‐hexane: DCM (90:10, v/v) to get hydrocarbons and alcohols followed by _n_‐hexane:DCM:MeOH (10:80:10, v/v/v) to get alcohols and acids.
Lipid Molecular Identification and Quantification

An aliquot of each fraction (1 mL) was silylated before chromatographic analysis to get trimethylsilyl derivatives by a reaction with 50 µL of N, O‐bis (trimethylsilyl) trifluoroacetamide (BSTFA), and 50 µL of pyridine at 70°C for 20 min.
The fraction was analyzed using gas chromatography‐mass spectrometry (GC‐MS; Agilent 6890 GC‐Agilent 5973 mass selective detector, MSD) equipped with electron impact (70 eV).
A silica capillary column (Restek, 30 m × 0.25 mm coated with RX‐5 stationary phase) was used with He as a carrier gas and with splitless mode.
The oven temperature program was: 70°C (2 min) to 210°C at 5°C min−1 to 300°C at 3°C min−1 (held 10 min).
Compounds were assigned using the NIST library (ver. 2008), retention times, authentic standards, published spectra, and fragmentation patterns.
An internal standard of _n_‐dodecane was spiked into an aliquot of each fraction at a known concentration before quantification.
The peak area of compounds was normalized to that of the internal standard and quantified to mass quantities calibrated by standard response curves.

External standards for instrument response calibration comprised _n_‐hexacosane, _n_‐eicosanoic acid, _n_‐tetracosanoic acid, gibberellic acid A3, oleanolic acid, and ergosterol, analyzed at a concentration ranging from 20 to 100 μg mL−1.
The quantified concentrations were normalized to the extracted mass of dry leaf materials which was reported as μg g−1 dry leaf.

Statistical Analysis
We performed all the statistical analyses in JMP 15 Pro (SAS, Cary, USA) and SPSS (Ver. 28; IBM).

To optimize modeling results, correlations between the lipid molecules and leaf‐level light irradiance (light transmittance, LAI sites) and leaf water content (RWC) and the overstory environmental factors (free‐air monthly _T_ max and monthly LAI) were assessed using both univariate and multivariate linear regression analysis in SPSS.
To assess the impacts of seasonality and topography on individual leaf lipid molecules, the one‐way multivariate of variance (one‐way MANOVA) was applied using SPSS.
The statistical results were reported under all the statistical assumptions fulfilled in the SPSS.
In the multivariate analysis, we used a Stepwise method.
Any coefficient of Pearson Correlation higher than 0.6 was excluded from the analysis.

We performed an analysis of MANOVA (General Linear Model) and Tuckey HSD (all pairs) using the SPSS to evaluate the seasonal differences of leaf lipids with leaf‐level environmental factors across three topographic positions (upland _n_ = 2, midslope _n_ = 2, lowland _n_ = 1).
Seasonal Canopy and Climatic Conditions Across the Study Site
Seasonal Understory Leaf Relative Water Content (RWC) Differed by Topographic Gradients
The seasonal RWC for _Q. buckleyi_ and _J. ashei_ decreased from the lowland to upland sites (Figures 2c and 3c; Supporting Information S1: Table S1–S3).
The seasonal variations of RWC in _Q. buckleyi_ and _J. ashei_ in the upland were significantly lower from that in the lowland (Supporting Information S1: Figure S2).
By comparison, the RWC for _Q. buckley_ i showed little seasonal fluctuation at all topographic positions (Supporting Information S1: Figure S2).
For example, the RWC in _Q. buckleyi_ was ~90% from April to July while RWC in _J. ashei_ decreased from ~80% to ~68% as hot and dry summer progressed (Figures 2c and 3c).

The low seasonal fluctuation in RWC was observed for _Q. buckleyi_, whereas, _J. ashei_ had a decreasing RWC through the growing season that corresponded to summer drought, demonstrating different water‐use strategies by the species (Figures 3c and 8).

Increasing free‐air temperature during the growing season affected leaf relative water content (RWC) probably via a stomatal closure to maintain a relatively high water content through the growing season (_Q. buckleyi_) or probably remaining stomatal open resulting in lower leaf water content as a response to the elevated evapotranspiration stress (_J. ashei_).
Correlation between RWC and leaf cuticular wax for _Q. buckleyi_ was strong and significant only in the droughty summer months while that for _J. ashei_ only occurred in Spring (April).
Summer free‐air temperature regulated the correlation between the leaf area index measured at each sampling point (LAI sites) and leaf wax, phytosterols, and/or isoprenoids for both species.

The free‐air temperature controlled the variation of unsaturation of fatty acids in _Q. buckleyi_ but this correlation was compromised as elevation increased while that in _J. ashei_ was not affected.

The RWC in _J. ashei_ was negatively correlated with monthly maximum free‐air temperature (_T_ max), despite differences in topographic location (Figure 3f; Supporting Information S1: Table S3), while this correlation was not observed for _Q. buckleyi_.
A positive RWC–monthly precipitation correlation for both species was observed, however, only for the trees located at the upland site (Figures 2i and 3i).
Seasonal precipitation variation affected RWC for both species likely due to very shallow soils at the upland location (< 10 cm).
Leaf‐Level Irradiance Changed Seasonally Across Topographic Gradients
For the lowland and midslope sites, the LAI sites decreased through spring to summer with the minimum values (~4.0) observed at the end of the growing season for both species.
The upland LAI sites remained at values ≤ 4.0 throughout the growing season for both species (Figures 2a and 3a).
Seasonal variability in leaf‐level light intensity also differed by topographic position (Figures 2a and 3a; Supporting Information S1: Table S3 and Figure S3).
The highest light transmittance occurred during summer months, ranging from 0.1 to 0.8, for both species across all sites (Figures 2b and 3b).
The variability in leaf‐level light was attributed to changes in LAI sites affecting transmitted irradiance through the upper canopy.

For _Q. buckleyi_, the leaf‐level light irradiance, as a function of LAI sites, was negatively related to _T_ max (Figure 2d,e) and positively with precipitation (Figure 2g,h), at the lowland and midslope sites.
The LAI sites–_T_ max relationship in _Q. buckleyi_ inferred that the species shed its leaves to reduce the transpiration rate caused by the rising _T_ max, VPD, and high light (Figure 8).

This relationship was not observed in the upland probably due to the relatively sparse canopy of this topographic position, which was significantly different from that in the midslope (_p_< 0.05, all pairs, Tuckey, HSD; Supporting Information S1: Tables S2 and S3).
A positive linear correlation between LAI sites and precipitation was observed at all three topographic positions in _J. ashei_ (Figure 3g).
LAI is associated with site water balance which is important for plants (Grier and Running 1977).
The seasonal LAI sites–precipitation relationship found for _J. ashei_, reflects the topographically constrained water availability.

Similarly, the positive intra‐seasonal LAI sites–RWC relationship was observed in the drought summer (Supporting Information S1: Figure S5), infers that a denser upper canopy is likely associated with greater site water availability reducing evaporative stress in the understory associated with lower leaf irradiance and possibly cooler temperatures (Supporting Information S1: Figure S4) (De Frenne et al.2013).
Leaf Lipids Differ by Species and Season
Important leaf lipids determined by those that varied significantly with environmental variables (Table 1) differed by tree species.
The observed seasonal lipid changes were associated with leaf relative water content (RWC) and LAI.

For leaf waxes, the lipids responding to the environment were _n_‐Heptacosane (_n‐_ C 27) and _n_‐Tetradecanoic acid (C14:0) for _Q. buckleyi_ in contrast to _n_‐Hentriacontane (_n‐_ C 31) and _n_‐Octacosanol (C28‐ol) for _J. ashei_.
Phytosterols were only found to respond significantly in _Q. buckleyi_ leaves including Stigmasterol and β‐Sitosterol.
For _J. ashei_, terpenoids including the sesquiterpenoid β‐Eudesmol and diterpenoid Dehydroabietane varied in the species but not in the oak.

The Leaf Wax and Phytosterols Varied With Intra‐Seasonal Leaf Water Content Rather Than the Whole Growing Season

The accumulation of longer _n_‐alkanol chains with low monthly precipitation in spring for _J. ashei_ and in late summer for _Q. buckleyi_ (Table 1 and Figure 8) implied that the chain length was altered by intra‐seasonal leaf water content (Chen et al.2020; Dimopoulos et al.2020).
The accumulated leaf wax _n‐_ C 27 in _Q. buckleyi_ captured the summer leaf water deficit rather than the whole growing season across the topographic positions.
Leaf wax is a layer between plants and the atmosphere, that the plant changes in its composition to reduce water loss (Chen et al.2020).
The content of leaf waxes, including _n_‐alkanes (C 27–C 33, odd), _n_‐alkanols (C 26–C 32, even), and short‐chain _n_‐alkanoic acids (C 14 and C 16), was increased with low monthly precipitation.
Alkane‐ and alcohol‐forming pathways and associated genes (e.g., _MYB96_) are upregulated by plant water stress and likely involved in wax biosynthesis (Lee, Kim, and Suh 2016; Jiang et al.2022).
Here, we observed a reduction in the concentration of stigmasterol with increasing water deficit, particularly for _Q. buckleyi_.
This is similar to a study of leaves for another angiosperm tree, tea (_Camellia_ spp.), that showed stigmasterol abundance decreased at the beginning of water deprivation (Chen et al.2020).

This is likely due to the conversion of β‐sitosterol to stigmasterol by desaturation of the hydrocarbon chain at C 22 which is suppressed by the low monthly precipitation during summer drought (August).

This aligns with the variation of phytosterols observed in _Q. buckleyi_ as β‐sitosterol was largely accumulated concurrently with a slight increase of stigmasterol in August (Supporting Information S1: Figure S13).
Seasonal Dynamics of Leaf Wax Reflect Distinct Understory Microclimatic Conditions
Higher irradiance due to more open canopies could cause chain lengths of leaf waxes to shift toward shorter homologs (e.g., C 28, C 29), as shown in other studies (Shepherd et al.1995,1997).

In _Q. buckleyi_ leaves, the shift of leaf wax _n_‐alkanoic acids to shorter homologs with higher irradiance during the dry summer months implying a combined influence of seasonal light and leaf water availability on the chain lengths (Supporting Information S1: Figure S8).

The longer chain _n_‐alkanoic acids (≥ C 20) are initially biosynthesized from saturated and monounsaturated C 16 and C 18 fatty acids produced in the plastid, which was activated as acyl‐CoAs by long‐chain acyl‐CoA synthetases in the cytosol and elongated to saturated long chain fatty acyl‐CoA products by fatty acid elongase complexes localized in endoplasmic reticulum membranes (Schnurr, Shockey, and Browse 2004; Samuels, Kunst, and Jetter 2008).

One of the core elongase enzymes involved in sequential elongation reactions is β‐Keto‐acyl‐CoA Synthase (KCS), which determines the substrate specificity of chain length in each reaction (Joubès et al.2008; Batsale et al.2021).
The expression of _KCS_ genes is shown to be influenced by light intensity and upregulated by dehydration (Joubès et al.2008).

We observed that the concentration of longer _n_‐alkanoic acid homologs (≥ C 20) in the dry, summer months was significantly higher than in the rest of the months (_p_< 0.005, all pairs, Tukey HSD) (Supporting Information: Figure S9).
The shift of ACL _n_‐alkanoic acids values may implicate KCS enzymes selecting shorter chain substrates at a higher light and low precipitation and high temperatures.

The accumulated shorter‐chain C14:0 in _Q. buckleyi_ was observed at the higher light (Figure 5b) while a long‐chain _n‐_ C 31 in _J. ashei_ decreased at the higher light in the droughty summer months (Figure 5h).
We attribute this to the combined effect of higher seasonal irradiance, low monthly precipitation, and high temperatures.
Shorter‐chain leaf wax (< C 28) (alkanes, alcohols, acids) in kale and swede leaves (_Brassica_ spp.) appears to be dominated in higher light intensity (Shepherd et al.1995).
The content of shorter‐chain SFAs (e.g., C14:0, C16:0) has been shown to increase with increased plant water deficit in _Arabidopsis thaliana_ and apple leaves (Kosma et al.2009; Jiang et al.2022).
Studies showed that core proteins involved in biosynthesizing the long‐chain _n_‐alkanes were regulated by water stress and light intensity (Bourdenx et al.2011; Wu et al.2022).

The decline in the amount of long‐chain C28‐ol in _J. ashei_ leaves appeared to result from an increased irradiance primarily observed in the summer and following winter when upper canopy LAI sites were lower (2.0 to 5.5) (Figure 5f,g,j; Supporting Information: Figure S10).
This C28‐ol–LAI sites change occurred with different _T_ max (37°C vs 17°C) and RWC (68% vs. 83%, on average) between the summer and winter months (Supporting Information S1: Table S1).
This implies that alcohol biosynthesis is mainly regulated by light intensity.

The KCS involved in the biosynthesis of long‐chain _n_‐alkanol precursors (long‐chain SFAs) was positively correlated with the abundance of C28‐ol in _Medicago ruthenica_ leaves (Guo et al.2021) with its transcriptional expression regulated by light intensity (Joubès et al.2008).
The higher concentration of C28‐ol in winter than in summer might benefit from a higher RWC and lower _T_ max besides the primary light intensity influence.

The long‐chain _n_‐alkanols (e.g., C 26, C 28, C 30) are biosynthesized via an acyl‐reduction pathway involving fatty acyl reductase enzymes located in the endoplasmic reticulum, resulting in an accumulation of cuticular waxes which are the critical constituents in the cuticle to respond to the stresses (Zhang et al.2022).

For example, the reduction of the content of long‐chain alcohols (C 28 and C 30) in cotton leaves (_Gossypium hirsutum_ L.) was observed under water deficit conditions (Yang et al.2022) while the freezing tolerance in the transgenic _Arabidopsis_ was increased by increasing the primary alcohols (i.e., _n_‐alkanols) (Zhang et al.2007).
Chain Lengths of Leaf Wax _n_‐Alkanols Respond to Seasonal Variations in Overstory Canopy Structures
The chain lengths of leaf wax were altered by the leaf light intensity.

The _Q. buckleyi_ leaves accumulated longer chain _n_‐alkanols (higher ACL _n_‐alkanols values) as the canopy opened over the growing season, at all three topographic positions, implying that this shift was related to the seasonal LAI variation rather than the local light regimes at the different topographic positions (Table 2 and Figure 6d–f).

As the enzymes involved in the biosynthesis of _n_‐alkanols are sensitive to light and/or selected specific chain lengths as their substrates (Giese 1975), there is a possible connection between canopy development and enzyme activation.

For example, C26‐ol in leaf wax of barley (_Hordeum vulgare_) is abundant in the light while decreased in the dark and was accompanied by an increase of the shorter chains (C 22, C 24) due to the light sensitivity of enzymes involved in the homolog biosynthesis (Giese 1975).

Also, the distribution of the _n_‐alkanols was altered by an expression of alcohol‐forming genes (e.g., FARs) at leaf emergence, for instance, the content of C28‐ol was significantly decreased while with an increase of C24‐ol in the flag leaves of wheat (_Triticum aestivum_) as compared with that in seedling leaves (Wang et al.2016).

However, we observed that the long‐chain _n_‐alkanol concentrations (C 32 and C 34) in _Q. buckleyi_ drastically increased after prolonged hot and dry summers (September and October, Supporting Information S1: Figure S7).
Together, the biosynthesis of long‐chain _n_‐alkanols was probably recorded in the canopy openings and lower leaf water content.
Seasonal Changes in Leaf Terpenoids Reflecting a Changing Microclimatic Environment Affected by Overstory Climate

The changes in phytosterol ratios were attributed to the decrease of stigmasterol in _Q. buckleyi_ within a certain summer light regime, implying a synergistic effect of the light and temperature on the sterols (Supporting Information S1: Figure S14).
Phytosterols are utilized by plants to alter various metabolic processes in response to light and temperature stresses by changing sterol contents and ratios (Aboobucker and Suza 2019).
In our study, the biosynthesis of stigmasterol appears to have been affected by the summer light but not β‐sitosterol for _Q. buckleyi_ (Supporting Information S1: Figure S15).
This result is intriguing given that sterols are considered to biosynthesize from the same pathway (Rogowska and Szakiel 2020).

High β‐eudesmol (oxygenated sesquiterpene) in _J. ashei_ with higher transmitted irradiance at 33°C (June) (Figure 5a) implied that its biosynthetic pathway might be light‐ and temperature‐dependent (e.g., Rivasseau et al.2009) (Supporting Information S1: Figures S11 and S12).

In contrast, the negative slope of the dehydroabietane (abietane‐like diterpene)–LAI sites relationship in _J. ashei_ was observed at 26°C (October), probably suggesting that the change of dehydroabietane was mainly affected by transmitted irradiance and temperature rather than water deficit.
Leaf Fatty Acid Unsaturation and Diterpenoid Responses to Air Temperature Differed By Topography
We found that the unsaturation of fatty acids decreased at higher air temperatures over the growing season with species and topographic position dependencies (Figures 6 and 7).
For _Q. buckleyi_, the upland site showed a stronger response to temperature concerning lower leaf UFAs amounts than the SFAs.
This is likely due to differences in understory temperatures resulting from higher transmitted light at the top of slopes (Figure 2).

SFAs are critical membrane components that are important for reducing membrane fluidity and increasing stability under high temperatures (e.g., Berg, Tymoczko, and Stryer 2002; He and Ding 2020; He et al.2020).

Plant plasma membrane compositional change includes the expression of genes involved in the biosynthesis of linoleic acid (C18:2) that is downregulated by high temperature resulting in a lower UFA content (Hernández et al.2011; Dar et al.2017).

For our site, we propose that the sparse canopy of the upland sites (LAI sites< 4.0; Figure 2a) over the growing season probably results in a smaller temperature difference between the understory and free‐air temperatures (Chen et al.1999; De Frenne et al.2013).
Here, the understory cooling measured in September was 0.8°C in the upland while that in the lowland was 2.6°C (Supporting Information S1: Figure S4).
Cooler understory temperature in the lowland in the summer might be attributed to the denser overstory canopy intercepting more solar irradiance (LAI sites> 4.0; Figure 2a) (De Frenne et al.2013).
In _J. ashei_, pimarane‐type diterpenoids correlated with _T_ max regardless of the topographic position.
The accumulated pimarane‐type diterpenoids in the higher temperature probably suggested its role in plant defense‐ and ‐ecological adaptation (Pelot et al.2018).

Diterpenoids are biosynthesized from the geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP), bicyclized to labdadienyl/copalyl diphosphate (CPP) intermediates, and then diversified by a series of diterpene synthases (diTPSs) (Zerbe and Bohlmann 2015).
Sandaracopimaradiene is converted from the CPP by specialized diTPSs (Pelot et al.2018).

It has been shown that the _ent_‐sandaracopimaradiene in rice (_Oryza sativa_) leaves serves as a precursor of phytoalexins (e.g., kauralexin and dolabralexin) (Wickham and West 1992), which were accumulated under drought and oxidative stresses (Pelot et al.2018).

Here, the accumulated sandaracopimaradienol (functionalized) may suggest a role against oxidative stress caused by the elevated temperature, implying that the accumulated pimarane‐type diterpenoids in _J. ashei_ may serve a protective role for both temperature and water stress.
Implication for the Use of Leaf Lipid Analysis in Terrestrial Ecosystem Studies
Leaf cuticular waxes have been applied to reconstruct past terrestrial ecosystems.
The ACL _n_‐alkanes is a proxy for water availability to correlate with mean annual precipitation and plant water (Shi et al.2021).
However, it is affected by plant species, temperature, and humidity (Feakins et al.2016; Eley and Hren 2018).
We observed that ACL _n_‐alkanols (_n_‐alkanols) values rather than the ACL _n_‐alkanes (_n_‐alkanes) were also influenced by intra‐seasonal leaf water and differed in plant species.

For example, the ACL _n_‐alkanols values (up to 3 carbons) in _J. ashei_ were changed with the RWC but only in April (Supporting Information S1: Figure S6), probably suggesting that the shift of chain lengths during the wax biosynthesis in evergreen species was recorded leaf water variation at early growing season rather than the entire growing season.

Here, our study demonstrated that the molecular response phenomena of native plant species (_Q. buckleyi_ and _J. ashei_) to the understory environmental variables were also affected by ambient climatic factors in the overstory as summarized in Figure 8.
Importantly, changes in leaf lipid molecular composition, observed within a single growing season, were correlated with changing environmental and climatic variables.

Under a naturally complicated combination of understory and overstory climatic conditions, we observed that the long‐chain leaf waxes, phytosterols, and terpenoids (C 15 and C 20) responded to monthly understory climatic conditions rather than the whole growing season climates while the leaf fatty acid unsaturation responded to air temperature differed by topographic gradients (Figure 8).

We also acknowledge that controlled experiments to determine the impact of each physiological factor on the leaf‐level metabolites are needed on the native plant species in the different canopy positions.

This study systematically investigated the regulation of seasonal overstory environments on the understory environment and the potential mechanisms of their impacts on understory leaf lipid profiles (Figure 8).
The results illustrated that _Q. buckleyi_ and _J. ashei_ with different seasonal leaf water content exhibit differing biomolecular responses to the intertwined overstory and understory environments.
Several insights into the responses of plants to the dynamic terrestrial ecosystem have emerged from this study.
Seasonal leaf RWC in _J. ashei_ was correlated with the free‐air temperature despite the topographic position, which was not observed in _Q. buckleyi_.
Also, the RWC was correlated with seasonal precipitation but only at sites with a sparse canopy, regardless of the species.
Seasonal physiological responses impact the leaf lipid profiles.

The long‐chain leaf waxes (≥ C 27) and stigmasterol in _Q. buckleyi_ captured RWC variations in the mid‐late growing season while the shift of chain length of leaf wax _n_‐alkanols in _J. ashei_ was only varied with the RWC in the early growing season.

The overstory canopy cover and leaf‐level irradiance values measured at the two species were related to the seasonal free‐air temperature and/or precipitation, which influenced the leaf lipids in response to the local light regimes at three different topographic positions and LAI at the site.
The composition of leaf wax was correlated with monthly variations in irradiance and the associated parameter, leaf water availability.
The abundances of isoprenoids (phytosterols, sesqui‐, and di‐terpenoids) were affected by the irradiance coupled with the seasonal free‐air temperature over the mid‐late growing season.
This points to the fact that the responses of those leaf lipids may be regulated by different combinations of the local light regimes, leaf water status, and free‐air temperature.
However, for _Q. buckleyi_ in the understory, the ACL _n_‐alkanols values captured a variation of the seasonal LAI, regardless of the local micro‐light regimes at the different topographic positions.

The unsaturation of fatty acids exhibited a strong correlation with the seasonal free‐air temperatures for both species, but the correlation in _Q. buckleyi_ was compromised by the temperature in the understory caused by the topographic position and regional LAI.

For _J. ashei_, a significant correlation between the diterpenoids (pimarane‐type) and the free‐air temperature was observed over one growing season, despite the possible temperature heterogeneity in the understory caused by the topographic position and canopy cover.
